newsitem.title: USA: Time Warner loss narrows in second quarter.
newsitem.headline: Time Warner loss narrows in second quarter.

text.p: Entertainment giant Time Warner Inc. said Wednesday that it more than halved its second-quarter net loss as its cable television, film and publishing businesses turned in stronger performances.
The company said its net loss shrunk to $49 million from $110 million a year ago, which included an extraordinary charge of $9 million from paying off debt.

More importanly, the company's closely watched cash flow -- earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA -- rose to $1.31 billion from $1.03 billion. Revenues rose to $5.92 billion from $4.75 billion.
The results cheered investors, who sent the company's stock shooting up by $4.375 to $49.75 in heavy trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the most actively traded issues.
"The (cash flow) numbers were great and above our estimates," said Jessica Reif Cohen, an analyst at Merrill Lynch. "All divisions looked very strong."
Analysts said they were especially surprised by the strength of the company's cable television networks, such as HBO, CNN, TNT, TBS, and the Cartoon Network.
The cable systems, which have about 12.4 million subscribers, kicked in a record combined $554 million in cash flow, up from $494 million.
Cash flow at the TBS networks jumped 41 percent to $186 million from a pro forma $132 million, and HBO increased cash flow to $103 million from $87 million.

"The surprise is the ongoing strength at Turner," said Chris Dixon at PaineWebber. "This is really a confirmation of the strategy ... to use the branded networks to drive new sources of revenues and find outlets for their entertainment production."
The increase at TBS, which Time Warner acquired from Ted Turner last year, was fuelled by "significant gains" in advertising revenues and improved subscription revenues, the company said.
"Time Warner is on track to have its strongest year of growth since its creation," Chairman Gerald Levin said in a statement.
"In the second half, we will continue to grow our business, while remaining focused on accelerating our return on capital in order to improve the overall capitalisation of Time Warner," Levin said.
Analysts said the company could generate more than $5 billion in cash flow this year, with the cable networks kicking in about $1 billion, including HBO.
However, debt remains an overall drag on profits.

"I don't think there was ever a question of whether this was a solid business, and that they could put up excellent growth numbers," said David Doft at Furman Selz. "But there's still a lot of debt on the balance sheet."
The company spent about $303 million in the quarter to cover interest and other payments. Analysts expect interest payments to total $1 billion for the year.
The company said its Time Inc. publishing business hit a record $174 million, up 12 percent.

The Warner film unit posted a record $155 million in cash flow, up 10 percent. TBS's filmed entertainment business, helped by the movie "Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery," had cash flow of $31 million vs. negative $21 million.
However, Warner Music Group's second-quarter cash flow fell to $125 million from $165 million due to declines in both domestic and international sales.
Analysts said Warner Music, which was hurt by a dearth of big-selling artists, was suffering from weak sales in a poor retail climate.
